decisions.reason: Dependent type and original identity: The paper collects new experimental data from 321 Slovak participants to re-test the published finding of Carr & Steele (2010, Study 2a; DOI: 10.1177/0956797610384146, 'Stereotype threat affects financial decision making'), so record_type is 'replication' and the target identity in row 2431 (paired with blind target 0) is resolved and confirmed. Outcome: The authors state an explicit overall verdict in the Abstract (lines 30-32), Discussion (p. 244, lines 1078-1082), and Conclusions (p. 247, lines 1208-1211) that their study failed to replicate Carr & Steele's (2010) finding on the effect of stereotype threat on women's risk aversion (rejecting hypotheses H2 and H3 across three risk elicitation methods, including the original Porcelli & Delgado lottery task, and across implicit and explicit threat conditions). Under Step 3 Rule 1 of the codebook, this explicit overall verdict governs and establishes the outcome 'failed'.

In the Introduction (p. 223), Theoretical Background (p. 228), Results (Table 2 on p. 233 and Step 1 regressions in Tables 8-9 on pp. 241-243), and Discussion (p. 246), the authors measure masculinity and femininity with the Bem Sex Role Inventory and financial risk attitudes (including Waerneryd's 1996 scale used by Meier-Pesti & Penz, 2008) to empirically test Meier-Pesti & Penz's (2008) finding that masculinity predicts lower financial risk aversion while femininity is unrelated to risk preferences, explicitly concluding: 'However, we did not corroborate this effect. Although our results show that biological sex is not predictive of risk aversion, unlike previous studies, we found that femininity alone weakly correlated with one of the risk aversion measures, while masculinity was unrelated to any of the measures.' The bibliographic identity is confirmed in the reference list (p. 250) and Crossref metadata (DOI 10.1016/j.joep.2007.05.002, Journal of Economic Psychology, 2008). It is absent from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2431, Carr & Steele, 2010, DOI 10.1177/0956797610384146) and is an independent primary study distinct from sibling target 3 (Lemaster & Strough, 2014).
